text: Under Section 3(p) of the Patents Act 1970, plants and animals in whole or any part thereof other than micro-organisms, including seeds, varieties and species, and essentially biological processes for production or propagation of plants and animals are NOT patentable in India. This means neem plant, tulsi plant, turmeric plant, ashwagandha plant, or any other medicinal plant CANNOT be patented as such. However, novel extraction processes, isolated compounds, or formulations using these plants MAY be patentable if they demonstrate novelty and inventive step.

Section 3(d) of the Patents Act 1970 prohibits patents on mere discovery of a new form of a known substance which does not result in enhancement of known efficacy, or mere discovery of any new property or new use of a known substance. For AYUSH products, this means you cannot patent a new form (salt, ester, polymorph) of a known Ayurvedic compound unless you prove enhanced therapeutic efficacy with clinical evidence. Simply discovering that an existing herb has a new use is not patentable.

Under Section 3(e), a mere admixture resulting only in aggregation of properties of components is NOT patentable. For Ayurvedic formulations, if you simply mix known herbs together and the result is just the sum of individual effects, it is NOT patentable. However, if the combination shows synergistic effect (enhanced efficacy beyond what individual components provide), it MAY be patentable with proper evidence.

Section 3(i) excludes from patentability any process for the medicinal, surgical, curative, prophylactic, diagnostic, therapeutic or other treatment of human beings or animals. This means Ayurvedic treatment protocols, Panchakarma procedures, or diagnostic methods CANNOT be patented. However, drugs, devices, and apparatus used IN such treatments CAN be patented.

Traditional Knowledge Digital Library (TKDL) contains over 3.5 lakh formulations from classical Ayurveda, Siddha, Unani and Yoga texts. Any formulation already documented in TKDL or classical texts like Charaka Samhita, Sushruta Samhita, or Ashtanga Hridaya is considered prior art and CANNOT be patented. Patent offices worldwide access TKDL to reject patents on traditional Indian knowledge. Before filing a patent on any Ayurvedic formulation, search TKDL to ensure it is not already documented.

Can I patent neem in India? No, you cannot patent the neem plant, neem seeds, or neem leaves as such under Section 3(p). Traditional uses of neem (as documented in Ayurvedic texts and TKDL) are prior art and not patentable. However, you MAY be able to patent: (1) A novel extraction process that is new and inventive, (2) A new isolated compound from neem not previously known, (3) A novel formulation combining neem with other ingredients showing synergistic effects with clinical evidence. The famous 1995 neem patent (EP0436257) by W.R. Grace was revoked in 2005 because the fungicidal use of neem was traditional knowledge in India.

Can I patent turmeric/haldi? The turmeric plant cannot be patented under Section 3(p). The wound-healing properties of turmeric are documented in TKDL and classical texts, so this traditional use is not patentable. The infamous 1995 US turmeric patent (US5401504) was revoked in 1997 after CSIR proved it was traditional knowledge. However, novel curcumin derivatives, new bioavailability-enhanced formulations, or new extraction methods MAY be patentable with proper evidence of novelty and inventive step.

Can I patent Ashwagandha? The Withania somnifera plant itself is not patentable under Section 3(p). Traditional uses documented in Ayurveda (stress relief, vitality enhancement) are prior art. However, patentable subject matter MAY include: novel withanolide extraction methods, new isolated withanolides not previously characterized, standardized extracts with specific withanolide ratios showing enhanced efficacy, or novel combinations with demonstrated synergistic effects.
